{{Short description|Concept in measure theory}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''varifold''' is, loosely speaking, a [[measure theory|measure-theoretic]] generalization of the concept of a [[differentiable manifold]], by replacing differentiability requirements with those provided by [[rectifiable set]]s, while maintaining the general algebraic structure usually seen in [[differential geometry]].  Varifolds generalize the idea of a [[Current (mathematics)|rectifiable current]], and are studied in [[geometric measure theory]].

==Historical note==
Varifolds were first introduced by [[Laurence Chisholm Young]] in {{harv|Young|1951}}, under the name "''generalized surfaces''".<ref>In his commemorative papers describing the research of [[Frederick J. Almgren Jr.|Frederick Almgren]], {{harvs|txt|first1=Brian|last1=White|author1-link= Brian White (mathematician)|year=1997|year2=1998|loc1=p.1452, footnote 1|loc2=p.682, footnote 1}} writes that these are "''essentially the same class of surfaces''".</ref><ref>See also the [https://www.dam.brown.edu/people/documents/Geometic_000.pdf 2015 unpublished essay] of [[Wendell Fleming]].</ref> [[Frederick J. Almgren Jr.]] slightly modified the definition in his mimeographed notes {{harv|Almgren|1965}} and coined the name ''varifold'': he wanted to emphasize that these objects are substitutes for ordinary manifolds in problems of the [[calculus of variations]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Almgren|1993|p=46}} exactly writes:-"''I called the objects "varifolds" having in mind that they were a [[Measure theory|measure-theoretic]] substitute for [[manifold]]s created for the [[Calculus of variations|variational calculus]]''". As a matter of fact, the name is a [[portmanteau]] of '''''vari'''ational'' ''man'''ifold'''''.</ref> The modern approach to the theory was based on Almgren's notes<ref>The first widely circulated exposition of [[Frederick J. Almgren Jr.|Almgren]]'s ideas is the book {{harv|Almgren|1966}}: however, the first systematic exposition of the theory is contained in the mimeographed notes {{harv|Almgren|1965}}, which had a far lower circulation, even if it is cited in [[Herbert Federer]]'s classic text on [[geometric measure theory]]. See also the brief, clear survey by {{harvs|txt|last=De Giorgi|first=Ennio|author-link=Ennio De Giorgi|year=1968|p=400}}.</ref> and laid down by [[William K. Allard]], in the paper {{harv|Allard|1972}}.

==Definition==
Given an open subset <math>\Omega</math> of [[Euclidean space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, an ''m''-dimensional varifold on <math>\Omega</math> is defined as a [[Radon measure]] on the set

:<math>\Omega \times G(n,m)</math>

where <math>G(n,m)</math> is the [[Grassmannian]] of all ''m''-dimensional linear subspaces of an ''n''-dimensional vector space. The Grassmannian is used to allow the construction of analogs to [[differential form]]s as duals to vector fields in the [[approximate tangent space]] of the set <math>\Omega</math>.

The particular case of a rectifiable varifold is the data of a ''m''-rectifiable set ''M'' (which is measurable with respect to the ''m''-dimensional Hausdorff measure), and a density function defined on ''M'', which is a positive function θ measurable and locally integrable with respect to the ''m''-dimensional Hausdorff measure. It defines a Radon measure ''V'' on the Grassmannian bundle of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>

:<math>V(A) := \int_{\Gamma_{M,A}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\theta(x) \mathrm{d} \mathcal{H}^m(x)</math>

where
*<math>\Gamma_{M,A}=M \cap \{x : (x, \mathrm{Tan}^m(x,M)) \in A \}</math>
*<math> \mathcal{H}^m(x)</math> is the [[Dimension (mathematics)|<math>m</math>−dimensional]] [[Hausdorff measure]]
Rectifiable varifolds are weaker objects than locally rectifiable currents: they do not have any [[Orientability|orientation]]. Replacing ''M'' with more regular sets, one easily see that [[Differentiable manifold|differentiable submanifold]]s are particular cases of [[Rectifiable set|rectifiable manifolds]].

Due to the [[Orientability|lack of orientation]], there is no [[boundary operator]] defined on the space of varifolds.

*{{Citation
|last = Almgren
|first = Frederick J. Jr.
|author-link = Frederick J. Almgren Jr. 
|title = Plateau's Problem: An Invitation to Varifold Geometry
|place = New York–Amsterdam
|publisher = W. A. Benjamin, Inc.
|series = Mathematics Monographs Series
|year = 1966
|edition = 1st
|pages = XII+74
|url = 
|mr = 0190856 
|zbl = 0165.13201
}}. The first widely circulated book describing the concept of a varifold. In chapter 4 is a section titled "''A solution to the existence portion of Plateau's problem''" but the stationary varifolds used in this section can only solve a greatly simplified version of the problem. For example, the only stationary varifolds containing the unit circle have support the unit disk. In 1968 Almgren used a combination of varifolds, integral currents, flat chains and Reifenberg's methods in an attempt to extend Reifenberg's celebrated 1960 paper to elliptic integrands. However, there are serious errors in his proof. A different approach to the Reifenberg problem for elliptic integrands has been recently provided by Harrison and Pugh {{harv|HarrisonPugh|2016}} without using varifolds.
